syllabus: SYNTHETIC TEST MATERIAL. CFA Level II Study Plan - Daniel. Created 2026-10-18. Target exam date: Saturday 2026-11-21 (5 weeks from today). Goal: score 75 percent or higher on both practice tests, finish every reading once and the weak topics twice. Study time: weekday evenings 1.5 hrs, Saturday 4 hrs, Sunday 2 hrs review. EXAM DOMAINS AND WEIGHTS (approximate, item set format): Ethical and Professional Standards 10-15 percent. Quantitative Methods 5-10 percent. Economics 5-10 percent. Financial Statement Analysis 10-15 percent. Corporate Issuers 5-10 percent. Equity Valuation 10-15 percent. Fixed Income 10-15 percent. Derivatives 5-10 percent. Alternative Investments 5-10 percent. Portfolio Management 10-15 percent. Priority topics: Equity, FSA, Fixed Income, Ethics and Portfolio Management, which together carry roughly 60 percent of the points. WEEKLY GOALS: Week 1 (2026-10-19 to 2026-10-25): Quantitative Methods (multiple regression, time series, intro to machine learning) and Economics (currency exchange rates, growth). Finish all end-of-reading questions with at least 80 percent accuracy. Week 2 (2026-10-26 to 2026-11-01): Derivatives (forwards, futures, swaps, put-call parity, binomial option pricing) and Fixed Income part 1 (yield curve, spreads, term structure models). Derivatives problem set due Friday 2026-10-30. Week 3 (2026-11-02 to 2026-11-08): Fixed Income part 2 (credit analysis, structured products) and Financial Statement Analysis (intercorporate investments, pensions, FX translation). Take Practice Test 1 on Saturday 2026-11-07, 4 hours, timed, in the morning. Week 4 (2026-11-09 to 2026-11-15): Review Practice Test 1 errors on Sunday 2026-11-08 and Monday, then Equity Valuation (DDM, free cash flow, residual income, market-based valuation) and Corporate Issuers (capital structure, M&A, dividends). Take Practice Test 2 on Saturday 2026-11-14. Week 5 (2026-11-16 to 2026-11-21): Portfolio Management, Alternatives, and a full Ethics review (Standards I-VII, case studies). Redo all flagged questions. Light review only on Friday 2026-11-20. Exam day: Saturday 2026-11-21, arrive at the test center by 7:30 AM. PRACTICE TESTS: Practice Test 1 on 2026-11-07 (target 65 percent or higher, expect weak spots in FSA and Derivatives). Practice Test 2 on 2026-11-14 (target 75 percent or higher). TRACKING: Log scores by topic in the spreadsheet every Sunday night. Any topic under 60 percent gets an extra 2-hour block the following Saturday. Flashcards for formulas (duration, convexity, Sharpe, Treynor, residual income, put-call parity) daily on the train, 15 minutes. Ethics question bank: 10 questions every weekday morning before work. Reminders: confirm exam registration and ID by 2026-11-01, buy calculator batteries (BA II Plus), print admission ticket by 2026-11-16. Take Sunday 2026-11-15 half off if tired, and keep sleep at 7 hours or more in the final week. Notes: ask study group about the Ethics case approach.
notes: Daniel - class notes wk 2. TOPIC 1: Multiple regression. Y = b0 + b1X1 + b2X2 + e. t-stat = (b - H0 value)/SE, df = n - k - 1. F-test tests if ALL slopes = 0 at once, one-tailed. R^2 always goes up when adding vars so use adj R^2. Problems: heteroskedasticity (resid var not const, SEs wrong, t-stats inflated, use Breusch-Pagan, fix w/ robust SE). Serial correlation (resids correlated, common in time series, Durbin-Watson, DW near 2 = ok, fix w/ Hansen SE). Multicollinearity (X vars correlated, high R^2 but low t-stats, VIF > 5 look closer, VIF > 10 bad, drop a var). Prof said look at the stem for hints, if the stem says high R^2 but nothing sig then think multicollinearity. Model misspec = omitted var, wrong form, pooled data. Influential obs: leverage vs Cook's D, Cook's D > sqrt(k/n) is flagged. TOPIC 2: Bond duration + convexity. Mod dur = Mac dur / (1 + y/m). Price change approx = -ModDur x dY + 0.5 x Convex x (dY)^2. Eff dur = (P- - P+) / (2 x P0 x dCurve). Use eff dur for bonds w/ embedded options, mod dur doesn't work there. Callable bond: neg convexity when yields fall, price compression, price capped near call price. Putable: pos convexity always, price floor. Longer maturity + lower coupon = higher duration. Money duration = ModDur x price. PVBP = money dur x 0.0001. Ex: ModDur 7.2, yld up 50bp, price chg approx -3.6 pct, convexity adds back maybe +0.2. Remember: convexity good for holder, benefits both directions. TODO: redo end of reading Qs 4-9, ask prof about key rate duration vs. effective duration, and review the DW table.
photoText: Residual Income Valuation (whiteboard, slide 12). RI_t = NI_t - (r x B_t-1) = (ROE - r) x B_t-1. Where r = cost of equlty, B = book vaue of equity. V0 = B0 + sum of RI_t/(1+r)^t. Steps: 1) forecast eamings and book value 2) deduct equity charge 3) discount residual income at cost of equity 4) add to currenl book value. Advantages: works w/ negatlve FCF, little reliance on terminal value. Drawbacks: relies on accountlng quality, clean surplus violatlons need adjustment [unreadable]. Persistance factor w: w=0 means RI drops to zero immed., w=1 means RI persists forever. Example: B0 = $40, ROE = 12%, r = 9%, RI1 = 0.03 x 40 = $1.20.
transcript: Okay, so, um, let's get started. Today we're talking about put-call parity, and, uh, this is one of those topics where, if you get the intuition, the formulas basically write themselves. So, um, imagine you have two portfolios. Portfolio one is a long call plus a bond that pays the strike price X at expiration. Portfolio two is a long put plus the underlying stock. Right? So, at expiration, what do these two portfolios give you? Well, if the stock ends up above the strike, the call is in the money, you exercise, and you have the stock, right? And in portfolio two, the put is worthless, but you still hold the stock. So both are worth S at expiration. Now if the stock ends up below the strike, the call expires worthless, and you have the bond paying X, so you get X. In portfolio two, you exercise the put, you sell the stock at X, so you get X. Same payoff in every state of the world. So, um, by no-arbitrage they must have the same price today. So that gives us: call plus the present value of X equals put plus the spot price. C + X/(1+r)^T = P + S. Okay, and this will be on the exam, so please, please be able to rearrange that in your sleep. You might need to solve for the call, for the put, or even for the implied risk-free rate. Um, so, uh, quick aside, did anybody else see the, uh, the marathon runners going past campus on Sunday morning? I almost got stuck in the road closure trying to get my coffee. Anyway, sorry, back to it. So, what do we do with this? One use is synthetic positions. So, a long call equals a long put plus long stock plus short bond, meaning you borrow the present value of X. And you can build a synthetic put too, by taking a long call, shorting the stock, and buying the bond. Now, the second use, and this is where the exam likes to go, is arbitrage. If the left side is more expensive than the right side, then you sell the expensive portfolio and buy the cheap one. You pocket the difference today, and at expiration the payoffs cancel out. So it's a risk-free profit. Um, let me do a quick example. Stock is at 50, strike is 50, rate is 4 percent, one year. The call trades at 6.00. Then put should be C + PV(X) - S, so 6 plus 50 divided by 1.04, which is about 48.08, minus 50, so about 4.08. If the put is actually trading at 5.00, it's too expensive, so you sell the put, short the stock... wait, no, let me redo that. You sell the put, you buy the call, you short the stock, and you lend the present value of the strike. Okay? And, um, so, you lock in about 92 cents today. Now, a few caveats. This is for European options, so no early exercise, and, um, no dividends, or else you have to subtract the present value of the dividends from the stock price. And for American options it's only inequalities, not equalities. Okay, so, an announcement before we finish: the Derivatives problem set is due Friday, October 30, by 11:59 PM, uploaded to the course portal. Late sets lose ten percent. I will also post the solutions to Practice Question 3 tonight. Okay, any questions? No? Alright, so, uh, for next time, read the binomial model section, and we'll do two-period trees. Thanks, everyone.
